MN202610_3tjic6uzm.t:
Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez is a four-weight world champion

Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez reclaimed the WBC super-middleweight title with a vintage performance against Christian Mbilli in Riyadh.

Just over one year since losing his belts to Terance Crawford, Mexican pound-for-pound great Alvarez returned to action with a confident victory by unanimous decision.

The 36-year-old, in his 69th professional fight, showed trademark slick defence and counter punching as he outclassed Mbilli to win 115–112, 116–111, 117–110 on the judges' scorecards.

It was the 64th victory of four-weight world champion Alvarez's illustrious career, while 31-year-old Mbilli suffered his first defeat in 31 bouts.

"It's so difficult to explain," said Alvarez.

"It's something unbelievable, this feeling. Like my first title. Thirty-one years as a professional. Sixteen years ago, I won my first title. Now, I won the title again. I'm so proud."

Doubts had been raised in recent weeks about whether the event could safely go ahead due to the growing conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi movement.

Just two days before the fight, Saudi Press Agency reported the Civil Defence had intercepted two ballistic missiles over Riyadh.

Earlier in October, a missile strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.

While other sporting events in Saudi Arabia - including The Six Kings Slam tennis exhibition, the final round of the 2026 World Rally Championship and the 2026 Urban Cycling World Championships - have been cancelled, the combat sports world has not followed suit.

Cameroon-born Mbilli, who trains in Canada, was making the first defence of his WBC title after being elevated to champion in January.

Alvarez, meanwhile, was competing for the first time without a world title to his name since 2015.

Pundits had questioned whether Alvarez's skills were declining following defeat by Crawford and over a year out of the ring, but his response was emphatic.

Mbilli pressured Alvarez in the early stages, peppering him against the ropes, with the Mexican looking to land big counters.

Alvarez responded by dismissively shaking his head to shrug off their impact, before goading Mbilli into attacking again.

Although Mbilli was throwing more punches, it was Alvarez who was landing the harder shots, with a couple of big right uppercuts finding the mark in round six.

The pattern continued in the next few rounds, with Alvarez countering the busy but largely ineffective Mbilli, before the defending champion was dealt a further blow by being docked a point for hits to the back of the head.

From there Alvarez cruised to the finish line with Mbilli continuing to push forward but posing little threat to the Mexican.

Alvarez's defence and timing of punches was too slick throughout, and although Mbilli landed a couple of stinging right hands in the closing stages, it was in vain.

Alvarez did not mention who he wants to fight next in his post-fight interview, but hinted at a quick return to training.

"I'm going to rest. I'm going to keep learning. I'm going to keep working hard," said Alvarez.

"And right now I'm going to be a couple of weeks off and then come back."

MN202610_u01bbknovi.t:
Huye: Umusore w’imyaka 23 yapfuye nyuma yo gukubitwa n’abaturage bamukekaho ubujura.

Abaturage bakubise uyu musore bamukekaho ko ngo yari agiye kwiba mu rugo mu Mudugudu wa Sata, Akagari ka Bukomeye, Umurenge wa Mukura, mu Karere ka Huye.

Bavuga ko uyu musore yinjiye mu rugo rw’umuturage utari uhari. Nyuma bene urugo n’abaturanyi bamubonye asohokamo, bakeka ko yari agiye kwiba, bahita bamukubita bikomeye, bigakekwa ko ari byo byamuviriyemo urupfu.

Umunyamabanga Nshingwabikorwa w’Umurenge wa Mukura, Karangwa Jean Baptiste, yemeza ibivugwa n’abaturage, akavuga ko bikimara kuba, Polisi y’u Rwanda n’Urwego rw’Igihugu rw’Ubugenzacyaha (RIB), ndetse n’izindi nzego bahise bahagera ngo hamenyekane uko ikibazo giteye.

Yagize ati: “Amakuru akimara kumenyekana, inzego z’umutekano n’iz’ubugenzacyaha zahise zihagera kugira ngo hakorwe iperereza.”

Umuvugizi wa Polisi y’u Rwanda mu Ntara y’Amajyepfo, CIP Hassan Kamanzi, avuga ko hatawe muri yombi umugabo w’imyaka 40 ukekwaho icyaha cyo gukubita no gukomeretsa byateye urupfu.

Uyu mugabo afungiye kuri Sitasiyo ya Polisi ya Ngoma, mu gihe Urwego rw’Igihugu rw’Ubugenzacyaha (RIB) rwatangiye iperereza.

Polisi isaba abaturage kwirinda kwihanira ahubwo mu gihe bahuye n’ikibazo bakakimenyesha ubuyobozi bukabafasha, ndetse no kujya batanga amakuru igihe bakeka ko hari icyaha cyakozwe.

Yagize ati: “Turakangurira abaturage kwirinda kwihanira. Umuntu ukekwaho icyaha agomba gushyikirizwa inzego zibishinzwe kugira ngo hakorwe iperereza, hamenyekane ukuri kandi ubutabera bukurikizwe.”

Akomeza kwibutsa abaturage ko gutanga amakuru ku gihe, no gukorana n’inzego z’umutekano ari byo bifasha gukumira ibyaha no kurinda ubuzima bw’abantu.

MN202610_1e0vjliog2c.t:
This year's Celebrity Traitors series saw 21 contestants slowly cut down to a final six

Spoiler warning: This story reveals details of The Celebrity Traitors final

The winners of Celebrity Traitors have said they are relieved that they no longer need to keep the biggest secret in British TV, as they reunited to celebrate their victory.

Actor Sebastian Croft and comedian Romesh Ranganathan were the last ones standing, with the two faithfuls splitting the £83,000 prize pot between their chosen charities.

"I am feeling good, it's so nice to finally be able to talk about it properly," Croft, known to pals as Bash, told BBC Newsbeat.

The second series of the hit BBC One show finished on Friday, after the original 21 celebs were whittled down to seven finalists.

Reuniting with Ranganathan on the comedian's BBC Radio 2 show on Saturday morning, Croft said they had been worried about being seen together in public before the final.

"We were having dinner and we're not exactly a likely duo and the whole restaurant was like, 'we like you on Traitors and hope you win'," he said.

Croft added that he had woken up on Saturday "with a light sense that I don't have to keep the secret anymore. It's been killing me".

Ranganathan, 48, started his show by saying: "Last night, I don't know if you're aware, was the finale of The Celebrity Traitors and I won."

He said he was "delighted to win" but admitted he probably wouldn't have done so without Croft convincing him to banish the last remaining traitor, King Kenny.

"It's taken the gloss off it slightly that everybody's saying, 'you better thank [Croft] every day for the rest of your life'," he added, with his typical deadpan-humour.

But 24-year-old Croft said he thought Ranganathan had played the game in a "lovely" way.

"People are seeing how smart you are and how you're actually so on it, and you're such a good judge of character," he praised.

What just happened in The Celebrity Traitors final?

The finale drew an average audience of 11.2 million live viewers, and that number will rise when fans catch up on iPlayer. Other recent episodes have been watched by more than 15 million, including catch-up.

"It's been a wild thing to be part of. To be on Uncloaked and sat with Romesh talking about winning was so surreal," Croft said, referencing the BBC's spin-off chat show.

"It's an out of body experience," he added.

Celebrity Traitors comes to a climax in nail-biting final

Croft said he "really wanted to be a traitor", but he turned out to be one of the strongest faithfuls after voting out Kenny - a tactical decision on how to play the show's famous endgame.

"The truth is, I didn't know for sure, but what you're trying to do isn't find a traitor, it's trying to get rid of everyone who isn't the most faithful," he explained.

"I think for both Maya [Jama] and Kenny there was no big thing where I was like 'they're obviously a traitor', but when you boil it down they haven't done anything that's really stuck out enough to make them obviously faithful."

Croft told Newsbeat that he gets why "people are obsessed with the show" and even his family had their own theories about how the game would go.

"So many people get so invested and it's lovely because it becomes so much bigger."

Romesh Ranganathan and Sebastian "Bash" Croft celebrate with host Claudia Winkleman

The final saw the celebs successfully banish the remaining traitors - Love Island host Maya Jama and YouTuber King Kenny.

But Kenny shocked viewers when he turned on his fellow traitor Jama at the final round table.

Asked if he's spoken to her since then, Kenny joked that "she's blocked me on everything", and then admitted that he had pre-warned her.

"I already told her that I was going to vote for her and she knew potentially that could be coming," he said.

"It was just too obvious, if I didn't go for her at that point, I think my time would've been coming even quicker than when I went out."

King Kenny turned on his fellow traitor Maya Jama in the tense finale

Kenny said he "experienced everything possible in the game" after starting out as a faithful, getting a shield to protect him from murder and then being recruited as a traitor.

But he said he "should have had a better plan for the final" and wasn't prepared for how hard it would be.

"There were so many times when I felt bad pinning stuff on people," he said. "It's a very draining thing to do as a traitor.

"There's moments when there is fun but lying to people for that long is insane, you build friendships as well and feel bad."

On his show, Ranganathan also asked fellow finalist, Little Mix singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock, about taking part in challenges while pregnant.

In the final episode, Pinnock was seen hanging off the side of a helicopter and lowering herself to the ground with a rope.

"I'm just super proud of myself," she said. "It's kind of just shown me that I really can do anything I put my mind to."

MN202610_10yn17jfxod.t:
Two major blockchain analytics firms say they have robust intelligence pointing to a North Korean state-backed group as the likely culprits in the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of Binance , the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.

The Lazarus Group, a North Korean hacking unit also known as TraderTraitor, was identified "with high confidence" by TRM Labs, as well as Chainalysis.

This incident is just the latest linked to the country, one of the poorest in the world and where access to the internet is severely restricted.

Experts accuse the government of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un of relying on cybercrime to finance itself, something Pyongyang has long denied.

Though not financial, the nation's most spectacular suspected hack took place in 2014. The target: Sony Pictures, which had made the Hollywood film The Interview. The film involves a plot to assassinate Kim.

The resulting hack exposed thousands of embarrassing emails exchanged among the studio's top executives.

Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far

Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea

Last year, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said North Korea was responsible for the theft of $1.5bn on the Bybit exchange.

In the aftermath of that incident, the agency said TraderTraitor had moved to quickly launder and disperse the stolen assets, converting them to Bitcoin and other digital assets with a goal of eventually turning them into hard currency.

The FBI has broadly accused North Korea of "illicit cybercrime and virtual asset theft activities".

The nation has systematically developed its cyber operations, recruiting the most promising students from universities and channeling them into hacker groups overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, according to reports.

Some of the cyberwarfare conducted takes place just over the nation's border in China, according to analysis from tech groups.

Watch: What we know about Binance's $6.3bn hack and what to do if you're affected

Much of its hacking activity has centred on monetary gain.

North Korean hackers are also suspected in the theft of $620m worth of cryptocurrency in 2022.

In this most recent heist, North Korean agents are accused of using a special authorisation to turn a Binance hot wallet, which is connected to the internet, into one that moved funds automatically to the attacker.

TRM said it's likely the attacker gained access to Binance's hot wallet signing system as part of the scheme.

Binance has not directly responded to the BBC's queries about the incident's potential links to the area.

The company had initially said it thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.

"Our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said.

Some 80% of stolen assets have been secured, a Binance spokesperson said on Friday, but the rest remains unaccounted for.

If the accusations are true, the record-making heist shows how powerful suspected North Korean hackers have become – a sign that the tools of the hacking trade have grown sharper.

Experts say the rise of artificial intelligence has also given threat actors new ways to carry out crime, through automation and other means.

In this case, it's plausible that AI was used to infiltrate Binance's systems.

As Chainalysis put it, the attacker used laundering patterns "we have not seen before".

MN202610_vp3z98wkd6.t:
Ndabashuhuje mwese mukurikiye BBC, none ni ku wa gatandatu tariki 31 y'ukwezi kwa 10 umwaka wa 2026, tugeze mu mwanya w'ikiganiro Imvo n'Imvano.

Turi mu gace ka Bugesera, ahazubakwa imihanda izajya ikinirwamo irushanwa rya Formula 1, ni nyuma yuko u Rwanda rwemejwe nk'igihugu kizakira irushanwa rya African Grand Prix mu gihe cy'imyaka 10 guhera mu ntangiriro ya za 2030.

Twasuye abatuye mu karere ka Bugesera ahazubakwa iyo mihanda, biteze kuhabona amahirwe menshi y'akazi. Bugesera iri mu birometero 40 uturutse mu murwa mukuru Kigali.

Uretse abo baturiye Bugesera, turumva n'abasesenguzi mu by'ubukungu batubwire uburyo aya marushanwa ashobora guhindura ubukungu bw'igihugu muri rusange.

Ese abasanzwe bakina umukino wo gusiganwa mu modoka mu Rwanda bo bariyumva bate mu mukino wa Formula1?

Abawuzi cyane na bo twabahaye ijambo, aho bavuga ko Formula 1 ari nk'igikombe cy'isi mu mupira w'amaguru ariko yo ikagira amategeko akakaye abawukina bagenderaho.

Ikiganiro cyo kuri uyu wa gatandatu mwagiteguriwe na Yves Bucyana.

MN202610_1mvmvjgfs0a.t:
Abategetsi bo muri Repubulika ya Demokarasi ya Congo (DRC) bavuga ko ubwoko bwa Bundibugyo bwa virusi ya Ebola ubu bufitanye isano n'impfu zirenga 5,000, intambwe iteye impungenge ku ngano n'ikwirakwira rikomeje kubaho ry'iki cyorezo.

Muri raporo ryatangaje ku wa gatanu, itsinda ryo mu biro bya perezida wa DRC rishinzwe ibikorwa byo kurwanya Ebola ryavuze ko abantu 10,351bamaze kwemezwa ko banduye Ebola kuva itangiye, barimo 5,026 bapfuye. Abategetsi bo mu rwego rw'ubuvuzi banatangaje ko abantu bashya 77 bemejwe ko banduye Ebola, naho abandi bantu 34 barapfa.

Iyo raporo igira iti: "Intara ya Ituri iracyari izingiro ry'iki cyorezo, ikaba yihariye 71.0% by'abantu bose bemejwe ko banduye batangajwe ndetse na 36.4% by'abantu bashya bemejwe ko banduye batangajwe ku rwego rw'igihugu."

Mu turere tw'ubuzima 178 twa DRC, 67 muri two twatangaje ko twabonetsemo abanduye Ebola. Iki cyorezo kimaze kugera mu ntara umunani muri 26 zigiye icyo gihugu, ndetse iki cyorezo gifite igipimo cyo kwica kiri ku rugero rwa 48.6%.

Abategetsi bo mu rwego rw'ubuvuzi bavuze ko abarwayi 1,101 ubu barimo kwitabwaho ahavurirwa Ebola no mu bigo by'akato, mu gihe abantu 2,788 bakize iyi ndwara.

Nubwo ibikorwa byo kurwanya Ebola bikomeje, umutekano mucye mu bice byo mu burasirazuba bw'igihugu byibasiwe n'iki cyorezo watumye akazi k'abakozi bo mu rwego rw'ubuzima kagorana. Mu duce tumwe, amatsinda yo kurwanya Ebola yashyizweho inkeke ndetse aterwa n'abantu badashyigikiye ingamba zo kurwanya Ebola.

Kugeza ubu nta rukingo rwemewe ruriho rw'ubu bwoko bwa Bundibugyo bwa virusi ya Ebola. Urukingo rwa Ervebo, rwakoreshejwe mbere mu byorezo by'ubwoko bwa Zaïre bwa virusi ya Ebola, buherutse gukoreshwa mu gufasha kurinda abaganga hamwe n'abakozi bakora mu bikorwa byo kurwanya Ebola aho yiganje.

Ishami ry'Umuryango w'Abibumbye ryita ku buzima (OMS/WHO) ryakomeje gusaba inkunga y'inyongera yo gufasha mu bikorwa byo kurwanya Ebola, mu gihe hari impungenge ko Ebola ishobora gukwirakwira ahandi kurushaho.

Ibihugu byinshi byo muri Afurika byakajije ingamba zo kugenzura no kwitegura Ebola, nyuma yuko umuntu wanduye Ebola aherutse kuboneka muri Nigeria. Uganda, Kenya n'Ubufaransa na byo byatangaje abanduye bafite aho bahuriye n'iki cyorezo muri rusange.

Amakuru y'inyongera yatawe na Emery Makumeno

MN202610_1kcropqkl6k.t:
Urukiko rukuru ku birebana n'ubutegetsi muri Repubulika ya Demokarasi ya Congo (DRC) rwategetse iseswa ry'ishyaka ryahoze riri ku butegetsi rya PPRD (Parti du Peuple pour la Reconstruction et la Démocratie), ryashinzwe n'uwahoze ari Perezida Joseph Kabila.

Igitangazamakuru cya leta n'ibindi bitangazamakuru byo muri DRC byatangaje ko urwo rukiko, rwitwa Conseil d'État, rurusha izindi ububasha mu by'ubutegetsi, rwafashe icyemezo gishyigikira ubusabe bwatanzwe na Minisitiri w'ubutegetsi bw'igihugu Jacquemain Shabani, wari wasabye urwo rukiko gusesa iryo shyaka ku mpamvu z'umutekano w'igihugu.

Ishyaka PPRD nta cyo ryahise ritangaza kuri icyo cyemezo cy'urukiko, urebye gishyize iherezo ku kubaho kwo mu rwego rw'amategeko kwa rimwe mu mashyaka ya politike yagize ijambo rikomeye cyane mu mateka ya vuba aha ya DRC.

Icyo cyemezo gikurikiye urukurikirane rw'ingamba leta yagiye ifatira ishyaka rya PPRD. Muri Mata (4) mu mwaka ushize, ibikorwa byaryo byabanje kuba bihagaritswe, mbere yuko muri Gicurasi (5) uwo mwaka Kabila ajya mu mujyi wa Goma mu burasirazuba bw'igihugu, icyo gihe wagenzurwaga n'umutwe w'inyeshyamba wa M23. Muri uku kwezi kw'Ukwakira (10), leta yongerereye igihe uko guhagarikwa kwa PPRD n'andi mashyaka ya politike 12.

Icyo cyemezo gifashwe nyuma y'ibyumweru birenga bibiri Kabila atangajwe ko ari we mukuru w'umutwe mushya w'inyeshyamba wa FRN (Front pour la Refondation de la Nation), ihuriro ririmo na M23, ushaka guhirika ubutegetsi bwa Perezida Félix Tshisekedi.

Mbere, abategetsi bo muri DRC bashinje Kabila wahoze ari Perezida hamwe n'ishyaka rye gukorana n'izo nyeshyamba. Mu gihe cyashize, Kabila na PPRD bahakanye ibyo birego.

Ishyaka rya PPRD, ryashinzwe muri Werurwe (3) mu mwaka wa 2002 mu gihe cya gahunda y'amahoro y'i Sun City muri Afurika y'Epfo, ryari ryo shyaka ryiganje muri politike yo muri DRC mu gihe cy'imyaka irenga 17, rigenda riyobora za leta (guverinoma) zagiyeho zivuye mu matora yo mu mwaka wa 2006 no mu 2011, nyuma riza gutakaza ubutegetsi ubwo Félix Tshisekedi yabaga Perezida mu 2019.

Abategetsi benshi bo ku rwego rwo hejuru muri iryo shyaka, barimo Aubin Minaku, Emmanuel Ramazani Shadary na Dunia Kilanga, baracyafunze ku birego birimo ubugambanyi n'ibyaha byibasira umutekano w'igihugu, ibirego bahakana bavuga ko bishingiye ku mpamvu za politike.

MN202610_1ezs8prl56l.t:
Joseph Kabila was a commander in the rebel alliance that brought his father to power in the Democratic Republic of Congo in 1997, went on to succeed him as president and now, at the age of 55, he is a rebel leader once again.

In an even stranger twist, the man he has sworn to topple is the very man he handed power to after 18 years at the helm, and with whom he had formed a coalition government after stepping down. While one of the rebel groups he had fought against as president is part of his new alliance.

His career reflects the ever-shifting nature of politics in DR Congo, where alliances are ephemeral, with the use of force a constant threat.

When Kabila was named leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), earlier this month, it confirmed what many Congolese had long believed – that the former president was working with the M23 rebels, who last year seized much of eastern DR Congo, including the region's main cities of Goma and Bukavu.

Nevertheless, the confirmation sent shockwaves through DR Congo – a vast country two-thirds the size of western Europe, with huge deposits of gold, diamonds and even more importantly minerals used to make everything from the mobile phones to batteries for electric vehicles.

For Kabila, the alliance offers a possible route back to the power he had lost.

For the M23 rebels, his involvement brings the experience and networks of a former head of state to a movement whose military advances have yet to translate into broad national legitimacy.

But it is far from certain that they can achieve their stated goal of ousting President Félix Tshisekedi.

Kabila (left) and President Tshisekedi entered a political coalition in 2019

Policy analyst Henry-Pacifique Mayala told the BBC that Kabila had been left with few options for regaining political influence.

"He actually was left with no other choice," he said.

Facing a death sentence after being convicted in absentia of treason, as well as US sanctions over his alleged support for the M23, Kabila may have sought assurances that the partnership could serve his interests, Mayala suggested.

"I'm not sure that he is making this huge leap in the dark without having received considerable assurance," Mayala said, adding that the M23's military strength could give Kabila greater leverage in any future negotiations with the Congolese government.

Kabila's involvement also raises questions about whether the conflict could spread beyond the east.

The M23's territorial gains have been concentrated in the country's eastern provinces, some 1,500km (1,000 miles) from the capital, Kinshasa.

Kabila's political networks could give the rebellion a broader reach, but that does not necessarily mean it has the capacity to extend its military campaign across the country.

And it is not clear how far Kabila's national reach extends.

While he was in power, after being named following the mysterious assassination of his father Laurent in 2001, he was often seen as something of an outsider in Kinshasa. He was far more at home speaking Swahili, the lingua franca of eastern DR Congo, as well as east Africa, rather than the Lingala spoken in Kinshasa.

His father's rebel group actually walked across the country to Kinshasa, also starting in the east, over a period of seven months, before eventually seizing power in May 1996 and ousting long-time ruler Mobutu Sese Seko, who had governed the country as his own personal property for more than 30 years.

There is little suggestion that Joseph Kabila's FRN would try to repeat that feat but earlier this week, he likened Tshisekedi to Mobutu.

"You have a tyrant who wants to impose and dictate what he thinks is right and not necessarily follow the constitution, which is the supreme law of the land," he told Conspiracy Trackers Great Lakes (CTGL), a pro-M23 research group.

DR Congo is rich in minerals such as the gold these women are looking for

Kabila accused the government of using the death penalty, ending the moratorium introduced during his own presidency, to intimidate civilians, politicians and members of the military, as well as himself.

He framed his confrontation with Tshisekedi as a fight against authoritarianism, invoking Section 64 of the constitution, which calls on citizens to resist anyone who seizes power or exercises it in violation of constitutional provisions.

Tshisekedi is rumoured to be planning to change the constitution to allow him to seek a third term in office, with the C64 coalition of opposition parties named after that same section of the constitution, campaigning against such a move.

But in a sign that he may not get everything his own way, the C64 coalition this week refused to back Kabila's rebellion, saying that Congo's multiple security crises cannot be resolved by military means alone. Instead, it announced plans to seek direct talks with both Tshisekedi and Kabila in pursuit of what it called a "genuine and inclusive national dialogue".

Richard Moncrieff, a Great Lakes analyst with the International Crisis Group think-tank, said President Tshisekedi retained substantial advantages.

"Tshisekedi has strong American backing. He has a lot of money. And he generally controls the political system and, as far as we can see, the military system," Moncrieff said.

In his first public reaction to Kabila being named FRN leader, Tshisekedi was damning: "In my view, it's simply proof that he has never loved this country, and even less its inhabitants," he said last week.

And yet Kabila is widely believed to have helped ensure that Tshisekedi succeeded him, rather than Martin Fayulu, who was the true winner of the 2018 elections, according to leaked results provided by the Catholic Church, which had observers around the country.

Former election chief Corneille Nangaa is one of Kabila's deputies

Indeed, the former head of the electoral commission who announced Tshisekedi as the winner, Corneille Nangaa, has said as much.

Now one of Kabila's deputies in the FRN, he claimed that Kabila and Tshisekedi had reached a political agreement before the final election results were announced.

"I can confirm that I helped draft the deal," Nangaa told France 24 in September 2023. "Tshisekedi is a liar. He knows there was an agreement and he knows what was contained in the deal."

Tshisekedi has maintained that he won the election legitimately.

What's the fighting in DR Congo all about?

How Trump wants the US to cash in on mineral-rich DR Congo's peace deal

After the disputed election, Kabila and Tshisekedi entered a power-sharing arrangement that allowed Kabila's coalition to retain control of parliament even after Tshisekedi took office in January 2019.

The arrangement unravelled in December 2020, when Tshisekedi moved to break Kabila's parliamentary dominance and build his own majority. The former allies became rivals, and Kabila went into self-imposed exile in South Africa.

From exile, Kabila's criticism of Tshisekedi grew louder.

He returned to DR Congo in 2025 and appeared in rebel-held Goma. In September that year, a military court sentenced him to death in absentia on charges including treason and financing violence in eastern Congo.

At the time, he rejected the accusations.

Yet another intriguing sub-plot to the announcement is Kabila's relationship with Rwanda's President Paul Kagame.

Presidents Kagame (left) and Tshisekedi signed a peace deal in Washington in November 2025, but fighting continues in eastern Congo

In the early years of his presidency, ties were strained between DR Congo and Rwanda, which accused its giant neighbour of not doing enough to remove ethnic Hutu militias involved in the 1994 Rwandan genocide from its territory. Their presence in what is now DR Congo has been used to justify Rwanda's repeated military involvement in its giant neighbour, going back to its backing of Laurent Kabila's rebellion.

The M23 was formed in 2012, vowing to stand up for the rights of ethnic Tutsis and to protect them against these militias, but also battling the Congolese army, under the control of Joseph Kabila.

From the start Rwanda was accused of backing them. It has always denied these allegations, as it still does despite overwhelming evidence.

However, relations later improved and Kabila's government worked with Rwanda against the Hutu militias.

Alex Vines, Africa programme director at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said Kabila's appointment as rebel leader could bring his interests into alignment with those of Rwanda's president, even though their objectives differ.

"Kabila wants to recover political influence nationally, while Kagame is primarily concerned with Rwanda's security and strategic position in eastern Congo. This is an alignment of convenience rather than a partnership built on deep trust," he said.

Policy analyst Mayala said Kabila's involvement could help Rwanda counter accusations that it was interfering in Congo's internal affairs.

"This is a former president. It's finally a Congolese rebellion," he said.

M23 rebels captured much of eastern DR Congo last year

Even before the announcement of Kabila as the rebellion's leader, fighting was continuing despite a peace accord overseen by Donald Trump last year.

Part of that deal saw the US sign an agreement to extract DR Congo's mineral wealth and the US has since seemed to side with Tshisekedi by imposing sanctions on various Rwandan officials and bodies, accusing them of prolonging the violence.

Elections are scheduled for 2028, but Tshisekedi has warned that fighting in the east could delay voting.

Against this backdrop, Kabila has questioned whether elections alone can resolve the country's political crisis.

"Does Congo need elections or a revolution?" he asked, arguing that lasting peace required a fundamental overhaul of the country's executive and legislature.

International security analyst Ovigwe Eguegu argues that Kabila is banking on military force to regain political influence, while Tshisekedi seems to be trying to extend his time in office beyond what the constitution allows.

"It looks like the Congolese people are going to lose either way, because neither of these two sides present a credible economic transformation plan for both the eastern Congo and the entirety of the country," Eguegu said.
